title: Asynchronous JS & Concurrency
description: Event loop microtask/macrotask queues, Promise combinators, concurrency pools, generators, and coroutine runners.

subtopics.title: Event Loop: Microtasks vs Macrotasks
subtopics.summary: Call Stack, Macrotask Queue (setTimeout/I/O), Microtask Queue (Promise.then/queueMicrotask), and UI render steps.
subtopics.mentalModel: The Event Loop continuously checks if the Call Stack is empty. When empty, it DRAINS THE ENTIRE Microtask Queue until empty (even if microtasks schedule more microtasks!) before picking ONE macrotask from the Macrotask Queue.
subtopics.traps: Microtask starvation (infinite `Promise.resolve().then(...)` locking the UI), order between `requestAnimationFrame`, `setTimeout(0)`, and nested `then` handlers.

questions.title: Microtask Runner with queueMicrotask
questions.concept: Microtask Dispatch Order vs Synchronous Execution
questions.problemStatement: Implement `runMicrotaskBatch(tasks)` that accepts an array of functions, executes them strictly as microtasks, and returns a Promise that resolves with an array of their results in order.
questions.interviewTrap: Assuming `queueMicrotask` executes in the next macrotask turn like `setTimeout`. Microtasks execute immediately upon completion of the current call stack.

testCases.name: Executes microtasks in parallel and returns results
testCases.testFn: return runMicrotaskBatch([() => 1, () => 2, () => 3]);

testCases.name: Handles empty task list
testCases.testFn: return runMicrotaskBatch([]);

testCases.name: Executes before setTimeout(0)
testCases.testFn: const log = []; await new Promise(r => { setTimeout(() => { log.push('timeout'); r(); }, 0); queueMicrotask(() => log.push('microtask')); }); return log;

details.name: Executes microtasks in parallel and returns results
Handles empty task list
Executes before setTimeout(0)

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: The JavaScript event loop processes tasks in phases: Synchronous code runs first to completion on the Call Stack, followed immediately by draining the entire Microtask Queue (Promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver), before the event loop advances to the Macrotask Queue (setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate, I/O).
stepByStepWalkthrough: Accept a callback function to run as a microtask.
Invoke `queueMicrotask(callback)` to enqueue the task into the microtask queue.
If `queueMicrotask` is unavailable, fallback to `Promise.resolve().then(callback)`.
Observe that the microtask executes immediately after the current synchronous script turn and BEFORE any macrotask (`setTimeout(0)`).
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In the HTML Event Loop specification (§8.1.6.3), the 'perform a microtask checkpoint' step runs whenever the JavaScript call stack becomes empty. The runtime loops over the microtask queue until it is completely drained, even if executing microtasks enqueue additional microtasks.

complexity.space: O(1) allocation in the engine microtask FIFO queue.

edgeCasesHandled: Executes ahead of macrotasks scheduled with `setTimeout(fn, 0)`.
Drains synchronously right after the enclosing synchronous execution block completes.
Errors inside microtasks are dispatched to global error handlers without halting queue draining.

specifications: HTML Living Standard §8.1.6.3 Perform a microtask checkpoint
ECMA-262 §9.5.4 Jobs and Job Queues (PromiseJobs queue)
MDN Web Docs: Using microtasks in JavaScript
verifiedRules: Microtasks execute at the end of the current task before yielding to rendering or macrotasks.
queueMicrotask is the standard explicit API for scheduling microtasks.

questions.title: Microtask Batcher (Coalesce Multiple Calls into Single Turn)
questions.concept: Event Loop Turn Coalescing & Batch Updating
questions.problemStatement: Build `createBatcher(flushCallback)` that batches multiple synchronous updates and triggers `flushCallback(accumulatedItems)` exactly ONCE in the microtask queue at the end of the current synchronous turn.
questions.interviewTrap: Calling the flush callback for every item or using `setTimeout` (which introduces a 4ms minimum delay and runs after UI rendering).

testCases.name: Batches multiple synchronous calls into one flush
testCases.testFn: const flushes = []; const batcher = createBatcher(items => flushes.push(items)); batcher(1); batcher(2); batcher(3); await Promise.resolve(); return flushes;

testCases.name: Subsequent turns trigger new independent batches
testCases.input: batch in turn 1 and batch in turn 2
testCases.testFn: const flushes = []; const batcher = createBatcher(items => flushes.push(items)); batcher(10); await Promise.resolve(); batcher(20); await Promise.resolve(); return flushes;

testCases.name: Flush receives full item set in exact insertion order
testCases.testFn: let res = null; const batcher = createBatcher(items => { res = items; }); batcher('a'); batcher('b'); batcher('c'); await Promise.resolve(); return res;

details.name: Batches multiple synchronous calls into one flush
Subsequent turns trigger new independent batches
details.input: batch in turn 1 and batch in turn 2

details.name: Flush receives full item set in exact insertion order

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A Microtask Batcher coalesces multiple synchronous calls made during the same event loop turn into a single batched flush executed in the subsequent microtask checkpoint, preventing redundant calculations or layout thrashing.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Maintain an internal array `items = []` and a boolean `scheduled = false`.
When `add(item)` is called, push `item` into `items`.
If `!scheduled`, set `scheduled = true` and schedule a flush via `queueMicrotask(flush)`.
In `flush()`, reset `scheduled = false`, snapshot `const batch = items.slice()`, clear `items = []`, and call `flushCallback(batch)`.
Subsequent calls in the next turn initiate a fresh independent batch.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: This is the exact mechanism React and Vue use for batching DOM updates and state setters. By leveraging `queueMicrotask` or `Promise.resolve()`, 100 synchronous state updates within one event turn collapse into exactly 1 re-render job.

complexity.time: O(1) per add operation; O(K) where K is batch size on flush.
complexity.space: O(K) temporary queue space in memory.

edgeCasesHandled: Multiple synchronous calls in the same turn execute only 1 flush.
Items are preserved in exact insertion order.
New items added in subsequent turns trigger a new batch cleanly.

specifications: HTML Living Standard §8.1.6 Event loops
React Architecture Docs: Batching state updates via microtasks
verifiedRules: Microtask coalescing aggregates synchronous operations into a single execution turn.
All synchronous script statements finish before the scheduled microtask executes.

questions.title: Microtask Starvation Guard & Fair Task Scheduler
questions.problemStatement: If recursive microtasks continually schedule more microtasks, the event loop locks up and macrotasks/UI renders never run. Implement `fairScheduler(tasks, maxMicrotasksPerYield)` that executes tasks via microtasks, but yields to a macrotask (`setTimeout`) after `maxMicrotasksPerYield` tasks to prevent UI starvation.
questions.interviewTrap: Infinite microtasks (`while(true) queueMicrotask(...)`) cause complete page freeze because the event loop will never leave the microtask checkpoint to service browser renders or user clicks.

testCases.name: Processes small batch without yielding
testCases.testFn: const tasks = [() => 1, () => 2, () => 3]; return fairScheduler(tasks, 5);

testCases.name: Processes large batch correctly with yields
testCases.testFn: const tasks = Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => () => i); const res = await fairScheduler(tasks, 3); return res.length;

testCases.name: Allows interleaved macrotask execution during yields
testCases.testFn: let timerFired = false; setTimeout(() => { timerFired = true; }, 0); const tasks = Array.from({ length: 8 }, () => () => 1); await fairScheduler(tasks, 2); return timerFired;

details.name: Processes small batch without yielding
Processes large batch correctly with yields
Allows interleaved macrotask execution during yields

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Because the event loop drains the microtask queue until it is completely empty before running any macrotask or browser rendering, recursively queueing microtasks causes *Microtask Starvation* (freezing the UI and starving I/O). A Fair Task Scheduler interleaves large batches by voluntarily yielding to the macrotask queue or scheduler API.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Process items in slices (chunk size, e.g. 10 items).
Process current slice synchronously.
If remaining items exist, check elapsed time or chunk limit.
Yield control to the macrotask queue using `await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0))` or `scheduler.yield()`.
This allows interleaved macrotasks (user input, timeouts, UI rendering) to execute before resuming the batch.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: The browser renders frames (requestAnimationFrame and Paint) between macrotask turns.Draining microtasks without yielding blocks the main thread completely. Yielding to a macrotask gives the browser event loop opportunity to process the UI and other tasks.

complexity.time: O(N) total processing time for N items.
complexity.space: O(N) memory for queued task items.

edgeCasesHandled: Interleaving allows macrotasks scheduled concurrently to execute.
Large tasks (e.g. 1,000 items) finish completely without freezing the thread.
Graceful completion on empty or single-item queues.

specifications: W3C Scheduling APIs: scheduler.yield() and Prioritized Task Scheduling
HTML Living Standard §8.1.6.2 Processing model (Macrotask vs Microtask starvation risks)
verifiedRules: Microtasks starve macrotasks if chained infinitely without yield.
Yielding via setTimeout(0) or scheduler.yield breaks synchronous task monopolization.

subtopics.title: Promise Internals & Concurrency Combinators
subtopics.summary: Promise state transitions, chaining return values vs thrown errors, implementing Promise.all / allSettled / race / any.
subtopics.mentalModel: A Promise is a state machine: [Pending] -> [Fulfilled] or [Rejected]. Once settled, state is immutable. Handlers registered via `.then` or `.catch` are always dispatched asynchronously as microtasks.
subtopics.traps: Forgotten `return` inside `.then` causing unhandled promises, uncaught rejections with `Promise.all` fast-failing, and handling non-promise values passed to combinators.

questions.title: Safe Promise Timeout Wrapper
questions.problemStatement: Implement `withTimeout(promise, ms, timeoutErrorMsg)` that returns a Promise that rejects with an Error(`timeoutErrorMsg`) if `promise` does not settle within `ms` milliseconds.
questions.interviewTrap: Not clearing the timer when the primary promise resolves or rejects, leaving open handles in server environments.

testCases.name: Resolves if promise completes before timeout
testCases.testFn: const p = new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('fast-result'), 10)); return withTimeout(p, 100);

testCases.name: Rejects with timeout error if operation takes too long
testCases.testFn: const p = new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('slow'), 100)); try { await withTimeout(p, 20, 'Timed out!'); return 'FAIL'; } catch (e) { return e.message; }

testCases.name: Preserves original promise rejection
testCases.testFn: const p = Promise.reject(new Error('original-error')); try { await withTimeout(p, 100); return 'FAIL'; } catch (e) { return e.message; }

details.name: Resolves if promise completes before timeout
Rejects with timeout error if operation takes too long
Preserves original promise rejection

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Network requests or asynchronous operations can hang indefinitely if servers stall. A Safe Promise Timeout Wrapper races an asynchronous promise against a timer promise that rejects with a `TimeoutError` if the specified duration expires first.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Accept `promise` and `timeoutMs` (duration in milliseconds).
Create a timer promise that sets a `setTimeout` to reject with `new Error('Timeout')`.
Use `Promise.race([promise, timerPromise])` to return whichever settles first.
Ensure the timeout timer is cleared via `clearTimeout` when the target promise resolves or rejects to prevent timer resource leaks.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: `Promise.race` attaches `.then()` handlers to all passed promises. Whichever settles first transitions the returned promise into fulfilled or rejected state. Subsequent completions of the other promise are ignored because a Promise can only transition state once (immutability of promise settlement per ECMA-262 §27.2).

complexity.space: O(1) memory for timer and race promise.

edgeCasesHandled: Fast operations resolve before timeout without penalty.
Slow operations reject with timeout error accurately.
Rejections from the target promise propagate immediately without waiting for timeout.
Timer handle is cleared to prevent keeping Node.js event loop alive.

specifications: ECMA-262 §27.2.4.5 Promise.race (Specification of race combinator)
MDN Web Docs: Promise.race & timeout patterns
verifiedRules: Promise settlement is irreversible once transitioned from pending.
Promise.race settles with the result of the first settled promise.

questions.title: Implement Custom Promise.allSettled
questions.problemStatement: Implement `myPromiseAllSettled(promises)` without using native `Promise.allSettled`. It takes an iterable of promises (or non-promise values) and returns a promise that resolves with an array of objects `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }` after ALL promises settle.
questions.interviewTrap: Using `Promise.all` which short-circuits on the first rejection. `allSettled` must wait for every promise regardless of success or failure.

testCases.name: Handles mix of resolved and rejected promises
testCases.testFn: return myPromiseAllSettled([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.reject('err'), 3]);

testCases.name: Handles empty array immediately
testCases.testFn: return myPromiseAllSettled([]);

testCases.name: Preserves exact order of input results
testCases.testFn: const p1 = new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('slow'), 30)); const p2 = new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('fast'), 5)); const res = await myPromiseAllSettled([p1, p2]); return res.map(r => r.value);

details.name: Handles mix of resolved and rejected promises
Handles empty array immediately
Preserves exact order of input results

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Implementing `Promise.allSettled` requires waiting for all promises in an iterable to settle (either fulfill or reject), returning an array of settlement descriptor objects in original order: `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Convert input iterable to an array `promises = Array.from(iterable)`.
If the array is empty, immediately resolve with `[]`.
Initialize an array `results = new Array(promises.length)` and `settledCount = 0`.
Iterate over promises with index `i`: wrap with `Promise.resolve(promises[i])` to handle non-promise values.
Attach `.then(value => { results[i] = { status: 'fulfilled', value }; checkDone(); }, reason => { results[i] = { status: 'rejected', reason }; checkDone(); })`.
In `checkDone()`, increment `settledCount++`. If `settledCount === promises.length`, resolve outer promise with `results`.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: Unlike `Promise.all` which fast-fails on the first rejection, `Promise.allSettled` never rejects. Results must maintain input indexing order even if promise 3 settles before promise 1.

complexity.time: O(N) where N is the number of promises.

edgeCasesHandled: Empty iterable resolves immediately with empty array.
Mix of fulfilled and rejected promises completes without short-circuiting.
Mix of raw values (primitives) and Promises handled safely via `Promise.resolve()`.
Preserves exact input order regardless of resolution timing.

specifications: ECMA-262 §27.2.4.2 Promise.allSettled
TC39 Proposal for Promise.allSettled (Championed by Mathias Bynens)
verifiedRules: Result objects adhere strictly to { status: 'fulfilled', value } and { status: 'rejected', reason } shapes.

questions.title: Throttled Promise Concurrency Pool
questions.problemStatement: Implement `promisePool(taskFns, concurrencyLimit)` that takes an array of promise-returning functions and executes them with at most `concurrencyLimit` tasks running concurrently. Returns a Promise resolving to an array of results in the original order.
questions.interviewTrap: Starting all promises simultaneously using `Promise.all(tasks.map(fn => fn()))` will overwhelm APIs or databases. Running workers that pull from a shared queue guarantees strict concurrency bounds.

testCases.name: Executes all tasks and preserves result order
testCases.testFn: const tasks = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4].map(n => () => Promise.resolve(n)); return promisePool(tasks, 2);

testCases.name: Enforces max concurrency limit
testCases.input: Never exceeds limit of 2 active tasks
testCases.testFn: let active = 0; let maxActive = 0; const makeTask = () => async () => { active++; maxActive = Math.max(maxActive, active); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 15)); active--; return 1; }; const tasks = [makeTask(), makeTask(), makeTask(), makeTask()]; await promisePool(tasks, 2); return maxActive <= 2;

testCases.name: Handles concurrency limit larger than task count
testCases.testFn: return promisePool([() => Promise.resolve('a'), () => Promise.resolve('b')], 10);

details.name: Executes all tasks and preserves result order
Enforces max concurrency limit
details.input: Never exceeds limit of 2 active tasks

details.name: Handles concurrency limit larger than task count

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A Throttled Promise Concurrency Pool executes a collection of asynchronous task factories with a strict maximum concurrency limit `concurrency` (e.g. running at most 3 HTTP requests concurrently). As each task completes, the next queued task starts immediately.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Initialize `results = []`, `executing = []`, and index `cursor = 0`.
Define an inner worker function that pulls the next task index from the shared cursor.
Execute task promise: `const p = Promise.resolve().then(() => taskFn())`.
Store the result in `results[currentIndex]` upon resolution.
When task finishes, remove its promise from the `executing` pool and trigger the next task from the queue.
Spawn `concurrency` initial workers simultaneously using `Promise.all(workers)`.
Return the collected results array when all tasks have settled.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: Unbounded parallel execution (`Promise.all(10000Requests)`) exhausts operating system socket file descriptors, saturates network bandwidth, and triggers HTTP 429 / ENOTFOUND errors. A worker-pool architecture maintains constant memory and socket pressure.

complexity.time: O(T / concurrency) total wall-clock duration where T is aggregate task time.
complexity.space: O(C) active concurrency promise allocations in memory where C is concurrency limit.

edgeCasesHandled: Task list smaller than concurrency limit runs all tasks without deadlocking.
Preserves exact output order matching task input indices.
Error in any task propagates rejection cleanly while ensuring active promises complete.
Concurrency limit is strictly never exceeded at any point in time.

specifications: Node.js Best Practices: Concurrency Limiting (p-limit pattern)
ECMA-262 §27.2 Promise Combinators
verifiedRules: Worker concurrency never exceeds configured integer bound.
Tasks execute continuously without idle gaps between resolutions.

subtopics.title: Async/Await as Generators + Promise Runners
subtopics.summary: Babel/TypeScript transpilation of async/await into `function*` and automatic Promise driver.
subtopics.mentalModel: Under the hood, `async/await` is syntactic sugar over Generator functions (`function*`) yielded to a coroutine runner that wraps each yielded value in `Promise.resolve()` and calls `generator.next(val)` or `generator.throw(err)`.
subtopics.traps: Sequential `await` in loops destroying parallelism (`for...of` vs `Promise.all`), unhandled errors silently terminating async chains.

questions.title: Infinite Sequence Generator with Step
questions.problemStatement: Implement a generator function `stepSequence(start, step, max)` that yields numbers starting at `start`, incrementing by `step`, until reaching or exceeding `max`.
questions.interviewTrap: Forgetting that generators are lazy; calling `stepSequence()` does not execute code until `.next()` is called.

testCases.name: Generates correct sequence from 0 to 6 with step 2
testCases.testFn: return Array.from(stepSequence(0, 2, 6));

testCases.name: Terminates when start > max
testCases.testFn: return Array.from(stepSequence(10, 1, 5));

testCases.name: Supports manual .next() consumption
testCases.testFn: const gen = stepSequence(5, 5, 20); return gen.next().value;

details.name: Generates correct sequence from 0 to 6 with step 2
Terminates when start > max
Supports manual .next() consumption

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Generator functions (`function*`) implement the Iterable and Iterator protocols (ECMA-262 §27.1). Unlike standard functions that run to completion, generators can pause execution via `yield` and resume when `.next()` is called, enabling lazy evaluation of infinite sequences without memory exhaustion.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Define generator `function* infiniteSequence(start = 0, step = 1)`.
Declare `let current = start`.
Enter an infinite loop: `while (true)`.
Execute `yield current` to pause execution and emit `{ value: current, done: false }`.
Upon resumption via `.next()`, update `current += step`.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: When a generator function is invoked, V8 does not execute its body immediately; instead, it returns an exotic GeneratorObject containing a heap-allocated Execution Context snapshot. When `.next()` is called, V8 restores the execution context onto the call stack, evaluates until the next `yield` bytecode, suspends the context, and returns the yielded value.

complexity.space: O(1) heap memory for the generator state object (does not allocate sequence elements in memory).

edgeCasesHandled: Zero step or negative step increments.
Infinite progression without memory leaks or call stack overflow.
Generates clean standard `{ value, done }` iteration protocol objects.

specifications: ECMA-262 §27.5 GeneratorFunction Objects and Iterator Protocol
V8 Dev Blog: Generator Suspension and Resume bytecodes (SuspendGenerator, ResumeGenerator)
verifiedRules: Generators pause at yield points without consuming CPU cycles.
Next invocation resumes from exact program counter and lexical scope position.

questions.title: Async Pipeline Generator
questions.problemStatement: Implement an async generator `asyncTransformStream(items, transformFn)` that consumes an array of items, applies async `transformFn(item)` to each sequentially, and yields each result.
questions.interviewTrap: Using `items.forEach(async ...)` inside an async generator does not pause generator iteration properly.

testCases.name: Transforms and yields items sequentially
testCases.testFn: const res = []; for await (const val of asyncTransformStream([1, 2, 3], async x => x * 2)) { res.push(val); } return res;

testCases.name: Handles empty array stream
testCases.testFn: const res = []; for await (const val of asyncTransformStream([], async x => x)) { res.push(val); } return res;

testCases.name: Handles async delays between yields
testCases.testFn: const res = []; const delay = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)); for await (const v of asyncTransformStream(['a', 'b'], async s => { await delay(5); return s.toUpperCase(); })) { res.push(v); } return res;

details.name: Transforms and yields items sequentially
Handles empty array stream
Handles async delays between yields

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: An Async Pipeline Generator combines async generators (`async function*`) with streaming data transformations. It yields items asynchronously, consuming upstream asynchronous data feeds with backpressure.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Define `async function* asyncPipeline(asyncIterable, ...transformFns)`.
Iterate over input stream using `for await (const item of asyncIterable)`.
Pipe the item sequentially through each transformation function: `let val = item; for (const fn of transformFns) val = await fn(val)`.
Yield the transformed value `yield val`.
Consumers pull transformed values one-by-one, pausing the upstream pipeline until requested.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: Async generators implement the AsyncIterator protocol (`[Symbol.asyncIterator]`), returning promises for each `{ value, done }` iteration step. This natively supports backpressure: if a downstream consumer is slow, the upstream generator waits at `yield` before pulling more data.

complexity.time: O(N * M) where N is item count and M is number of transform stages.

edgeCasesHandled: Empty stream produces zero yields and terminates with `{ done: true }`.
Asynchronous delays inside transform functions are properly awaited.
Errors in transforms reject downstream consumers safely.

specifications: ECMA-262 §27.6 AsyncGeneratorFunction Objects and AsyncIterator Protocol
WHATWG Streams Standard (Stream backpressure principles)
verifiedRules: Async iterators return a Promise resolving to an IteratorResult.
Execution only advances when downstream invokes .next(), providing natural backpressure.

questions.title: Implement 'co' / asyncToGenerator Coroutine Runner
questions.problemStatement: Implement `runCoroutine(generatorFactory)` which takes a generator function yielding Promises, steps through each yield sequentially passing resolved values into `.next(val)` and rejected errors into `.throw(err)`, and returns a Promise resolving to the generator's final return value.
questions.interviewTrap: This is the exact polyfill Babel generates for `async/await`. Candidates often fail to handle generator `.throw(err)` when a yielded promise rejects.

testCases.name: Steps through yielded promises sequentially
testCases.input: yield promise -> yield promise -> return sum
testCases.testFn: return runCoroutine(function* () { const a = yield Promise.resolve(10); const b = yield Promise.resolve(20); return a + b; });

testCases.name: Catches thrown errors inside generator try/catch
testCases.input: yield rejecting promise caught by generator try/catch
testCases.testFn: return runCoroutine(function* () { try { yield Promise.reject(new Error('fail')); } catch (e) { return 'caught-error'; } });

testCases.name: Propagates unhandled rejection to returned promise
testCases.input: unhandled rejected yield rejects coroutine promise
testCases.testFn: try { await runCoroutine(function* () { yield Promise.reject(new Error('unhandled-boom')); }); return 'FAIL'; } catch (e) { return e.message; }

details.name: Steps through yielded promises sequentially
details.input: yield promise -> yield promise -> return sum

details.name: Catches thrown errors inside generator try/catch
details.input: yield rejecting promise caught by generator try/catch

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Before `async`/`await` was standardized in ES2017, libraries like TJ Holowaychuk's `co` implemented async coroutines using generators and promises. `async`/`await` is syntactic sugar over generator coroutine runners (demonstrated by Babel's `asyncToGenerator` transform).
stepByStepWalkthrough: Implement `co(generatorFn)`: return a Promise.
Instantiate the generator: `const gen = generatorFn()`.

Define step runner: `function step(nextFn) { let res; try { res = nextFn(); } catch (err) { return reject(err); } if (res.done) return resolve(res.value); Promise.resolve(res.value).then(val => step(() => gen.next(val)), err => step(() => gen.throw(err))); }`.
Start execution with initial `step(() => gen.next())`.
If a yielded promise rejects, `gen.throw(err)` injects the error back into the generator's `try...catch` block!
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: When a generator yields a promise, execution suspends. The runner attaches `.then` callbacks to that promise. When resolved, `gen.next(value)` resumes the generator, passing the resolved value into the LHS expression `const x = yield promise`. If rejected, `gen.throw(error)` raises an exception at the exact `yield` expression line.

complexity.time: O(P) where P is the number of yielded promises + execution time of coroutine.
complexity.space: O(1) runner overhead beyond generator state.

edgeCasesHandled: Yielding non-promise primitive values wrapped automatically via `Promise.resolve()`.
Errors thrown inside generator or rejected promises propagate to `gen.throw()` or reject the returned promise.
Return values from generator fulfill the outer promise.

specifications: ECMA-262 §27.7 AsyncFunction Objects (Formal specification of async function evaluation as coroutine)
Babel Specification: babel-plugin-transform-async-to-generator
TJ Holowaychuk's co library source architecture
verifiedRules: async/await evaluates according to generator + promise reaction loop semantics.
gen.throw() faithfully injects exceptions into generator try/catch blocks.
